newsitem.title: USA: New allegations fly over Maine nuclear plant.
newsitem.headline: New allegations fly over Maine nuclear plant.

text.p: A Nuclear Regulatory Commission employee who oversaw regulation of the Maine Yankee power facility has alleged the plant lied about the adequacy of computer code used to test a key safety system, officials confirmed Tuesday.

Maine Yankee declined to comment on the allegatons by retired NRC project manager Patrick Sears, who also charged in a petition to the agency that problems with the computer code are "endemic to the industry as a whole."

Meanwhile, NRC officials refused to comment on a published report that the agency has placed its current project manager overseeing Maine Yankee on administrative leave for allegedly leaking the results of an investigation to plant officials.

Edward Trottier was suspended for allegedly giving Maine Yankee advance information on an NRC probe, according to the the industry newsletter "Inside NRC" - which did not specify what information was released to the company.

NRC last month completed an investigation into allegations by an anonymous whistleblower's that plant engineers fraudulently manipulated the test results. The probe's results are now being reviewd by the U.S. Justice Department.

Maine Yankee has denied wrongdoing involving tests of the cooling system and submitted new tests using a different computer model. The 910-megawatt has been limited to 90-percent capacity while the NRC reviews the new testing data.

Sears, who was the NRC official responsible for approving Maine's Yankee's testing, charges that a Maine Yankee engineer lied by claiming in 1989 that the computer code used to test the emergency core cooling system was "operable."

The code in question, RELAP, is used in computer models that test the adequacy of emergency cooling systems by simulating a reactor accident simular to that happened at the Three Mile Island power plant in 1979.

According to NRC documents, Sears' petition contends the NRC is aware there are "serious deficiences" with the code, and that Maine Yankee is not the only U.S. nuclear facility that used the code to test safety systems.

The NRC's inspector general complained in report in May that Sears and other members of the agency failed to adequately review Maine Yankee's testing or do follow-up checks to see if the plant was following safety requirements.
Sears contends in his petition that he was ordered not to do additional testing on the code.

Maine Yankee spokeswoman Maureen Brown said the plant could not comment on Sears' allegations because of the pending Justice Department Investigation. "We are aware of the allegations," Brown told Maine Public Radio.
Maine Yankee is 38 percent owned by Central Maine Power Co, 20 percent each by New England Electric System and Northeast Utilities, and 22 percent by other New England utilities.
